# Abstract {-}

**Background.** Treatment response in aggregated N-of-1 clinical
trials reflects three causally distinct mechanisms: pharmacological
action of the active compound (BR), the patient's belief that the
treatment will work (PB), and natural-history drift in the
underlying condition (TV). Standard analysis models combine these into
a single 'treatment effect' plus residual error. Whether this
one-component approach biases inference, and whether a component decomposition
repays its cost in degrees of freedom and power, is not
unconditional: it depends jointly on the estimand, on the trial
design, and on whether a candidate biomarker correlates with the
non-pharmacological components. This paper makes that dependence
precise and resolves it into a design-by-correlation-structure rule.

**Methods.** We formalize a three-component decomposition of the
within-participant outcome trajectory, each component a modified
Gompertz function with participant-specific random effects, and
characterize the trial-design contrasts (open-label, blinded
discontinuation, crossover, balanced-placebo) that supply
identifiability. We derive the omitted-variable-bias identity for
the one-component estimator, which expresses both the one-component
treatment effect and the one-component biomarker slope as sums of
component-specific terms. We then evaluate analysis strategies in
three Monte Carlo studies calibrated to the prazosin-PTSD reference
parameters: Study A couples the biomarker to BR only ($c_{bm,PB}=0$)
and varies the unmodeled-component magnitudes (1,000 replicates per
alternative cell, 5,000 per null, across $m_{PB} \in \{0,1,3,6,10\}$,
$m_{TV} \in \{-1,0,1,2\}$, $N \in \{35,70,100,150\}$); Study B
(100-replicate pilot) couples the biomarker to PB; and Study C
(1,000 replicates) contrasts the standard hybrid design with a
belief-decoupling balanced-placebo design across
$c_{bm,PB} \in \{0,0.1,0.2,0.3\}$.

**Results.** The identity shows that the one-component
biomarker-treatment slope is displaced from the pharmacological
slope by a term proportional to the biomarker's covariance with PB
and TV, not by the magnitude of those components; three regimes
follow. (i) *Biomarker orthogonal to PB and TV, hybrid design:* the
one-component estimator is essentially unbiased across the whole
grid (mean absolute bias $0.016$ at $N=35$, $0.006$ at $N=150$,
within one Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) of zero) and strictly more
powerful than the phase-augmented decomposition (mean power $0.59$
versus $0.35$ at $N=35$; $0.90$ versus $0.62$ at $N=70$);
decomposition removes no bias and only sacrifices power, so it is
dominated. (ii) *Biomarker coupled to PB, standard hybrid design:*
the one-component slope is biased in proportion to $c_{bm,PB}$
(one-component bias rising to $+0.48$, coverage falling to $0.86$ at
$N=150$), but because the drug-state and belief contrasts are
collinear under this design (analysis-stage correlation
$\approx +0.6$), no decomposition recovers the pharmacological slope
either. (iii) *Biomarker coupled to PB, balanced-placebo design:*
adding covert-drug and open-placebo phases decouples the contrasts
($\approx -0.66$), and the belief-covariate decomposition then
returns the unbiased pharmacological slope across the feasible
contamination range (bias within one MCSE of zero,
coverage $0.94$--$0.96$) where the one-component estimator does not,
at the cost of some power.

**Conclusions.** The benefit of decomposition is jointly determined
by the biomarker's correlation structure and the trial design, not
by either alone. When the candidate biomarker is orthogonal to PB
and TV, a single-indicator analysis that exploits the design
contrast is unbiased and most powerful, and a parametric component
model is counterproductive. When the biomarker may correlate with PB
or TV, the one-component slope is biased and decomposition is necessary, but
the bias is recoverable only under a design that varies belief
independently of drug exposure (balanced-placebo or open-hidden); on
the standard hybrid design no analysis recovers it, so a
biomarker-validation trial at risk of placebo-belief contamination
must be fielded with the decoupling design. Component decomposition
is likewise warranted whenever the estimand is the attribution of
response to pharmacology versus belief versus natural history. A
pragmatic specification for the cases that warrant it is
`Sx ~ bm + t + Dbc + phase + Dbc:phase + bm:Dbc + bm:Dbc:phase`
with random intercept and AR(1) residual correlation.

# Introduction

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Partitioning treatment response into pharmacological ($BR$), placebo-belief ($PB$), and natural-history ($TV$) channels has biological precedent and clinical appeal; this paper rigorously evaluates when the partition is worth making.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Precedent runs from pharmacometric disease-progression models [@holford2015; @gomeni2009] through Kaptchuk's empirical decomposition of the placebo response itself [@kaptchuk2008components] to neuroimaging dissociations of drug from expectancy effects [@wager2013nps; @zunhammer2018nps]; each motivates the partition on independent biological grounds.
\item Clinical appeal is direct: $BR$ is what persists after expectancy decays; $PB$ drives apparent response in high-placebo-responsiveness populations and misleads precision-medicine stratification when mistaken for pharmacological prediction; $TV$ is what would have changed without any treatment at all.
\item Partitioning costs degrees of freedom, requires specific trial-design contrasts for identifiability, and adds analytic complexity; whether the cost is warranted is an empirical and design-dependent question this paper answers.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}

:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Decomposing treatment response into pharmacological, expectancy,
and natural-history contributions is not a new idea.
Pharmacometrics has long modeled disease progression and drug
effect as separable longitudinal processes [@holford2015;
@gomeni2009]; Kaptchuk and colleagues decomposed the placebo
response itself into observation, ritual, and
practitioner-relationship components in a three-arm IBS trial
[@kaptchuk2008components]; neuroimaging has directly dissociated
pharmacological from expectancy-driven analgesia using objective
neural signatures [@wager2013nps; @zunhammer2018nps]. The
partition has intuitive clinical appeal: a patient whose symptom
improvement is pharmacological will benefit from long-term
treatment even after novelty fades, whereas one whose improvement
is primarily belief-driven may not sustain it as expectations
normalize. The question this paper addresses is not whether the
partition is biologically coherent -- it is -- but when it is
necessary for valid inference.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The optimal choice is conditional: decompose when the candidate biomarker may correlate with $PB$ or $TV$; use the one-component analysis when domain knowledge supports orthogonality.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Decompose: COMT val158met genotype as a biomarker in IBS or PTSD trials -- COMT regulates dopaminergic expectancy processing and is a documented predictor of placebo-response magnitude [@hall2012comt; @wang2022comt], making it a $PB$ moderator whose one-component biomarker-treatment slope conflates pharmacological and belief-driven prediction. Baseline symptom severity is similarly confounded: it predicts pharmacological response but also couples to regression-to-mean $TV$ [@hrobjartsson2001; @hrobjartsson2010] and heightened treatment expectancy [@kirsch2008; @locher2015].
\item One-component sufficient: CYP metabolizer phenotype as a pharmacokinetic biomarker -- enzymatic drug metabolism cannot plausibly couple to belief state or untreated disease trajectory, so the one-component pharmacological slope is already the target estimand. ADRB2 Arg16Gly in asthma bronchodilator trials provides an analogous case: the variant affects receptor downregulation via a direct pharmacological mechanism, lung function is objectively measured by spirometry, and no expectancy pathway links ADRB2 genotype to $PB$.
\item In the PTSD/prazosin context of this paper: baseline PCL-5 severity belongs in the decompose column (a psychological measure with documented coupling to both $PB$ and $TV$); an adrenergic receptor variant affecting prazosin binding affinity belongs in the one-component-sufficient column (pharmacological mechanism, no $PB$ coupling).
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The decision criterion follows from an algebraic identity
established in section 6: the one-component biomarker-treatment slope
decomposes as $\beta_{bm}^{\text{lumped}} = \beta_{bm}^{BR} +
w_{PB}\beta_{bm}^{PB} + w_{TV}\beta_{bm}^{TV}$, where the
loadings $w_{PB}$ and $w_{TV}$ are determined by the trial
design and the $\beta_{bm}^{C}$ terms are component-specific
slopes. Bias is zero if and only if $\beta_{bm}^{PB} =
\beta_{bm}^{TV} = 0$, that is, if and only if the biomarker is
uncorrelated with the non-pharmacological components. Whether
that condition holds is determined by biology and domain
knowledge, not by the magnitude of $PB$ or $TV$ in the study
population. A population with a large placebo response but a
biomarker orthogonal to it yields an unbiased one-component estimate;
a population with a small placebo response but a biomarker that
correlates with it yields a biased one.

COMT genotype exemplifies the first category. COMT modulates
catechol-O-methyltransferase activity in prefrontal cortex,
regulates dopaminergic signaling in expectancy circuits, and
predicts placebo-response magnitude in IBS and chronic pain
populations [@hall2012comt; @wang2022comt]. A trial using COMT
as a predictive biomarker for prazosin response would face a
one-component slope that conflates pharmacological prediction with
expectancy moderation. CYP2D6 metabolizer phenotype exemplifies
the second: the genotype determines hepatic drug metabolism and
thereby plasma drug concentration, with no plausible pathway
to expectancy or natural-history effects. ADRB2 Arg16Gly in
asthma bronchodilator trials provides a further example:
spirometric outcomes are objective and receptor binding affinity
does not modulate belief. For both, the one-component pharmacological
slope is already the target estimand.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{An algebraic identity establishes the conditional rule exactly; Study A confirms the orthogonal arm; Study B (pre-registered, pilot complete) addresses the coupling arm; together they bound the inferential cost of the choice.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The identity (section 6) is exact: bias in the one-component slope $= w_{PB}\beta_{bm}^{PB} + w_{TV}\beta_{bm}^{TV}$; it is zero if and only if the biomarker is orthogonal to $PB$ and $TV$, regardless of the magnitude of those components.
\item Study A (section 7.3; 1,000 replicates per alternative cell, 5,000 per null) confirms the orthogonal arm: mean absolute bias in the one-component $\hat\beta_{bm:D_{bc}}$ is $0.016$ against a true value of $-2.25$ at $N=70$, with no trend across $m_{PB} \in \{0,1,3,6,10\}$ or $m_{TV} \in \{-1,0,1,2\}$.
\item Study B (section 7.4; 100-replicate pilot reported here; production run pre-registered) addresses the coupling arm: pilot data show bias scaling with $c_{bm,PB}$, consistent with the algebraic prediction and motivating the production run.
\end{itemize}
:::

:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 fixes compact notation
and states the formal model. Section 3 develops each component
with biological motivation, parametric form, and identifiability
conditions. Section 4 maps the hybrid
open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design's phase structure
onto the decomposition's identifiability requirements. Section 5
develops the analysis-side methodology, including the
phase-augmented linear mixed-effects model (LME) approximation. Section 6 works through the
numerical illustration and derives the algebraic identity that
anchors the conditional rule. Section 7 presents Study A
(orthogonal arm) and the Study B pilot (coupling arm). Section 8
translates the conditional rule into a practical
biomarker-validation decision criterion under the PATH framework
[@kent2020path]. No published N-of-1 trial has applied this
evaluation framework; the paper's primary contribution is
determining when decomposition changes the inferential answer
rather than advocating for it as a universal default.
:::

# Notation and the formal model

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{This section fixes compact notation and states the formal model; a fuller worked-example treatment is in the companion pedagogical document.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Definitions are precise enough to support the identifiability and analysis-side arguments in later sections.
\item The presentation is kept compact; extended derivations are deferred to the companion document.
\item The companion pedagogical document provides numerical worked examples at each formal step.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
In this section we shall fix notation and state the formal
model. The three components are defined precisely enough to make
the identifiability and analysis-side arguments in later
sections rigorous, but we have endeavored to keep the
presentation compact. A fuller treatment, with worked numerical
examples at each step, is available in the companion pedagogical
document at \texttt{docs/24-component-decomposition-pedagogy.md}.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
where $Y_{it}$ is the observed symptom score, $\mathrm{BL}_i$
is participant $i$'s baseline score, the three components $BR$,
$PB$, $TV$ are non-negative reductions in symptom severity
attributable to the three causal mechanisms identified in
section 1, and $\varepsilon_{it}$ is observation-level noise.
The sign convention is that an increase in any component reduces
$Y$; all three components are zero at $t = 0$ by construction
(no exposure yet to drug, no belief activation, no elapsed
natural history) and grow over the duration of the trial.
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
For participant $i$ at trial timepoint $t$:

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \mathrm{BL}_i \;-\; \bigl[\,BR_{it} + PB_{it} +
TV_{it}\,\bigr] \;+\; \varepsilon_{it},
$$
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{Each component is driven by its own time-on-state variable, making the components structurally distinct even when they overlap in calendar time.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item $BR_{it}$ accumulates with time-on-drug; $PB_{it}$ with time-on-belief scaled by expectancy $\eta(\text{phase})$; $TV_{it}$ with calendar time from trial entry.
\item The distinct time indices are the structural source of identifiability from phase-contrast data.
\item All components are zero at $t = 0$ by construction and grow over the trial duration.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Each component is a participant-specific function of its own
time-on-state variable. $BR_{it}$ depends on time-on-drug, the
cumulative exposure to active medication since drug initiation.
$PB_{it}$ depends on time-on-belief, modulated by a
phase-specific expectancy factor $\eta(\text{phase})$ that
captures the patient's confidence that they are receiving active
treatment. $TV_{it}$ depends on time-since-trial-entry,
calendar time elapsed regardless of treatment status.
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
rescaled so that $C(0) = 0$ and $C(t) \to m_C(1 - e^{-d_C})$ as
$t \to \infty$, for $C \in \{BR, PB, TV\}$. The three Gompertz
parameters $(m_C, d_C, r_C)$ are participant-specific random
effects drawn from population distributions, and the
participant-level heterogeneity in these distributions is the
principal source of between-participant response variability that the
framework is designed to characterize.
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
Each component follows a modified Gompertz curve:

$$
C(t) \;=\; m_C \,\exp\bigl(-d_C \exp(-r_C t)\bigr) \,-\,
m_C\,\exp(-d_C),
$$
:::

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{The residual term has AR(1) structure and the three components are permitted to co-vary through cross-component covariances.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item Within-participant residuals follow $\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, \varepsilon_{i,t+h}) = \sigma^2_\varepsilon \rho^{|h|}$.
\item Within-time and across-time cross-component covariances permit participant-level heterogeneity in one component to co-vary with the others.
\item This structure accommodates biologically plausible correlations, such as high-$BR$ patients also tending toward high-$PB$.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit, sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua.
:::

::: {.orig data-latex=""}
$\varepsilon_{it}$ is a within-participant residual term with
AR(1) serial-correlation structure
$\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon_{it}, \varepsilon_{i,t+h}) =
\sigma^2_\varepsilon \rho^{|h|}$. The three components are
permitted to be jointly correlated through within-time and
across-time cross-component covariances $c_{cf1t}$ and
$c_{cfct}$ respectively, so that participant-level heterogeneity
in any one component can co-vary with heterogeneity in the
others.
:::

# The three components

::: {.bullets data-latex=""}
\textbf{This section presents each component with its biological motivation, Gompertz parameterization, and identifiability conditions to establish the model as causally interpretable.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}
\item The three components are presented in turn: $BR$ (biological response), $PB$ (placebo-belief), $TV$ (natural history).
\item Each component is grounded in independent biological literature before its parametric form is stated.
\item The section's purpose is to demonstrate that the model sum reflects causal structure, not mathematical convenience.
\end{itemize}
:::

::: {.rgt data-latex=""}
